catalog_quote: The main stress in Magahi words fall on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy; it falls on the ult syllable if the penultimate syllable is light. [...] The syllable weight appears to determine the stress system of Magahi. Therefore, Magahi seems to be a quantity-sensitive language. [...] If a word has a long vowel (V:) in the penult, it will receive penultimate stress [...] If a word has CVC syllable structure in the penult, it will receive penultimate stress. [...] The stress assigned to words with a word final CVC syllable depends on what precedes it. If it is preceded by a CV or a V syllable then the ult syllable gets the ultimate primary stress. [...] If a word is disyllabic with a CVC.CVC structure then he stress falls on the penultimate syllable. But if the disyllabic structure is CVC.CV:C then the stress falls on the final syllable. [...] The point is that the primary stress or the main stress of Magahi falls on the penultimate syllable in unmarked conditions which includes a heavy syllable structure at this position and a comparatively light syllable word finally. Another point that can be made here is that a final syllable can attract stress just in case it is not preceded by a heavy syllable. [...] 13. a) Foot Construction: Form moraic trochees from right to left. b) Extrametricality in Clash: Foot -> <Foot> / V: __]word c) Word Layer Construction: End Rule (Right)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and quantity-sensitive (Hindi/Maithili type): build moraic trochees right-to-left and stress the rightmost foot (End Rule Right), with a final foot made extrametrical when it would clash with a preceding heavy (CV: or CVC) penult. Net effect: a heavy penult (long vowel or closed) is stressed (sá:ri, bár.tan, tSam.gá.dar, di.még.wa); if the penult is light and the final is heavy the final is stressed (tSa.már, pa.ri.bár, u.khár); CVC.CV:C disyllables stress the superheavy final (bar.bá:d, khan.dá:n); light-light disyllables stress the penult (déekha 'see', /kala/). Stress is not phonemic; length is contrastive only marginally.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'The following structures suggest that Magahi has both primary as well as secondary stress' (p.74); non-head feet carry secondary stress, e.g. plural template kút.ˌwan, ka.gédʒ.ˌwan (HH / LHH with secondary on the final heavy, p.79); stress clash of adjacent stressed syllables is avoided (epenthesis, cluster avoidance).
new_statements.exceptions: A derivational stressed suffix /-á/ forming causative/intransitive-passive stems gives final stress in disyllables 'against the general rule where in a disyllabic word the stress is on the penultimate' (tSalá 'made to go' vs tSála 'let's go', p.68); stress described as partly 'morphologically or lexically conditioned' (p.70); unstressed vowels adjacent to the stressed syllable are attenuated/shortened or deleted (bihán ~ bíhne); CVC treated as heavier than CV: in clash contexts; loanwords repaired by epenthesis/metathesis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms from ~500-item basic word lists elicited from 12 native speakers aged 20-70; acoustic checks in Praat/Wavesurfer). In isolation the stressed syllable carries the intonational pitch accent (p.61); phrase-level rhythm and wh-question intonation treated separately in ch. 5-6. Variety: Magahi of Bihar generally; no sub-dialect singled out in the chapters read (author a native speaker).
new_statements.identity_note: Sinha 2012 describes Magahi (maga1260) as spoken in Bihar without singling out a sub-dialect in the chapters read; the author is a native speaker and data come from 12 native-speaker informants. A. C. Sinha 1966 describes 'a Magahi dialect' (unspecified in the pages viewed). Grierson 1903's accent rule is stated for Bihari as a whole (Maithili-Magahi-Bhojpuri), not Magahi specifically. Khortha/Eastern Magahi materials (LSI-Jharkhand, Dialectologia Khortha profile) concern a distinct variety and were not used.

new_statements.quote: In Magahi, stress placement and syllabic structure are closely linked to vowel shortening. Unless other factors like syllable weight and derivational structure interfere, the penultimate in disyllabic words and the antepenultimate in words with more than two syllables generally receive stress. Vowels in stressed syllables often have the longer allophone, whereas those in unstressed syllables have the shorter one. Heavy syllables are CVCC and CVC, where V stands for a diphthong or /a/. In disyllabic words, the stress would be shifted to the final syllable by a heavy final syllable; in trisyllabic words, the stress would be shifted to the penultimate by a heavy penultimate syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement (Sinha 2012: weight-sensitive, heavy penult stressed) and the catalog record has no rule text, so at the type level it agrees and adds detail (definition of heavy syllables, default positions by word length, stress-conditioned vowel attenuation, stress shift under suffixation). One detail differs from Sinha 2012: for words whose penult is light, Sinha 2012 (ch. 4 p. 70) puts main stress on the final syllable, whereas Kumar (after Verma 2007) gives penult (disyllables) / antepenult (trisyllables, e.g. /nokəri/) as the default and moves stress to the final syllable only when that syllable is heavy. Variety: Magahi of Aurangabad district, Bihar (the thesis's…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress is penultimate (= initial) in disyllables and antepenultimate in words of three or more syllables; a heavy syllable (CVCC, or CVC with a diphthong or /a/ as nucleus) pulls stress rightward: a heavy final syllable takes stress in disyllables (/bəsənt̪/ 'spring', /t̪õd̪əɪl/), a heavy penult takes stress in trisyllables; otherwise /səɽəl/, /ʈʰelaː/, /boːɟʰaː/ keep penult (initial) stress and /nokəri/ 'job' antepenult stress. Stressed vowels take the long allophone, unstressed (pre-tonic) vowels are attenuated/shortened (loːhaː ~ lohaːr, soːnaː ~ sonaːr, ɖaːka ~ ɖəkəit̪); suffixation re-computes stress (moʈəri ~ moʈərijaː). The section is an overview explicitly based on Verma (2007, 'Magahi' in Cardona & Jain), not an original stress analysis; ch. 4 (pp. 80-82) adds that diminutive /waː/ forms carry penultimate stress 'due to the heavy penultimate syllable' with shortening of the antepenult vowel, citing Sinha 2018.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Unless other factors like syllable weight and derivational structure interfere' - derivationally related longer words shift stress and undo attenuation (moʈəri vs moʈərijaː); vowel length is allophonic (length follows stress), so heaviness is defined by coda consonants and diphthong or /a/ nuclei only.
new_statements.identity_note: Kumar's fieldwork variety is Magahi as spoken in Aurangabad district, Bihar; the stress overview in section 1.4.7.5 is drawn from Verma (2007), a general description of Magahi, so it is not specific to that district.

sources.note: Full metrical analysis: stress non-phonemic, 'fixed, weight-sensitive'; main stress on the penult if heavy (CV: or CVC), on the final if the penult is light and the final is heavy; CV.CV disyllables penult; rules: moraic trochees right-to-left, extrametricality-in-clash of a final foot after V:, End Rule Right (compared explicitly to Hindi/Maithili per Hayes 1995); secondary stresses on other feet; exception: stressed derivational suffix -á (causative/passive) gives final stress in disyllables.

sources.note: General Bihari rule (p.24): 'As regards Accent, the general rule is to throw it back as far as possible.. The accent cannot be thrown further back than the antepenultimate, and if the penultimate is long the accent falls on it.' The Magahi section (p.35) says the Maithili vowel/unaccented-syllable remarks 'also apply to Magahi' but gives no Magahi-specific accent rule.
